original_value: Traditionally, motion planning involved navigating one robot from source to goal for accomplishing a task. Now, tasks mostly require movement of a team of robots to the goal site, requiring a chain of robots to reach the desired goal. While numerous efforts are made in the literature for solving the problems of motion planning of a single robot and collective robot navigation in isolation, this paper fuses the two paradigms to let a chain of robot navigate. Further, this paper uses SLAM to first make a static map using a high-end robot, over which the physical low-sensing robots run. Deliberative Planning uses A* algorithm to plan the path. Reactive planning uses the Potential Field Approach to avoid obstacles and stay as close to the initial path planned as possible. These two algorithms are then merged to provide an algorithm that allows the robot to reach its goal via the shortest path possible while avoiding obstacles. The algorithm is further extended to multiple robots so that one robot is followed by the next robot and so on, thus forming a chain. In order to maintain the robots in a chain form, the Elastic Strip model is used. The algorithm proposed successfully executes the above stated when tested on Amigobot robots in an office environment using a map made by the Pioneer LX robot. The proposed algorithm works well for moving a group of robots in a chain in a mapped environment.

result.paraphrase: Traditionally, motion planning meant guiding a single robot from a source to a goal to complete a task. Today, tasks often require a team of robots to move to a goal site, with robots arranged in a chain to reach the target. Although the literature separately addresses single-robot motion planning and collective robot navigation, this paper combines both paradigms to enable chained robot navigation. It also uses SLAM to create a static map with a high-end robot, on which the low-sensing physical robots operate. Deliberative planning employs the A* algorithm to compute the route, while reactive planning uses the Potential Field Approach to avoid obstacles and remain as close as possible to the initially planned path. The two methods are then integrated into an algorithm that lets the robot reach its goal along the shortest possible path while avoiding obstacles. The algorithm is further extended to multiple robots so that each robot follows the next, forming a chain, and the Elastic Strip model is used to preserve that chain structure. Tested on Amigobot robots in an office environment using a map created by the Pioneer LX robot, the proposed algorithm successfully performs as described and works well for moving a group of robots in a chain within a mapped environment.
